lesson.title: When Work Became a Wage: The Roots of American Labor Organizing
lesson.summary: As factories replaced small workshops in the decades after the Civil War, millions of Americans traded personal independence for wage labor, and out of the harsh conditions that followed grew the first organized efforts to demand better treatment.
lesson.body:
Before industrialization reshaped American work, many laborers experienced dependence in a very different form: indentured servitude, in which a person signed away years of their labor, often to pay for passage to the colonies, in exchange for room, board, and eventual freedom. That system had mostly disappeared by the nineteenth century, replaced by an ideology of free labor, the idea that American workers, unlike enslaved people or indentured servants, were free to sell their labor to whichever employer they chose and to quit whenever they wished. The rise of the factory system, described in the story of the Industrial Revolution in America, tested that ideal. Workers were legally free, but most had no real alternative to wage labor, no land of their own, no independent trade to fall back on, and no savings to survive without a paycheck. In practice, many factory workers found themselves as dependent on their employers as any servant had once been on a master, just without the legal bond and without any guarantee of continued work.

Conditions inside the new factories, mills, and mines were often brutal. Ten to twelve hour days, six days a week, were standard. Machinery had few safety guards, and injuries, even deaths, were common and rarely compensated. Children worked alongside adults for a fraction of the pay. Wages could be cut at an employer's discretion, and workers had almost no legal protections and no safety net if they were injured, laid off, or grew too old to work. Periodic economic depressions made things worse. The Panic of 1873 threw hundreds of thousands out of work and triggered wage cuts across whole industries, and the Panic of 1893 did much the same twenty years later, setting the stage for major confrontations like the Pullman Strike.

Workers began organizing to push back. The National Labor Union, founded in 1866 under the leadership of iron molder William Sylvis, was among the first attempts to unite workers nationally around shared goals, most notably the eight hour workday. It collapsed after the depression that followed the Panic of 1873, showing how fragile early labor organizations were. A more dramatic sign of worker anger came in 1877, when wage cuts on major railroads triggered the Great Railroad Strike, which spread from West Virginia across much of the country and became the first strike to shut down rail traffic on a national scale. State militias and federal troops were used to break it, and dozens of strikers were killed in the process. The strike failed, but it revealed both how widespread labor discontent had become and how far employers and government were willing to go to suppress it, lessons the next generation of labor organizations, beginning with the Knights of Labor, would try to learn from.
